title: Anti-aging effects of the adrenal androgens dehydroepiandrosterone and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate: mechanisms of action and beneficial effects in older people

sections.abstract:
We review the recent remarkable progress of the molecular mechanisms of action of the adrenal androgens dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) regarding their beneficial effects on older people and adrenal regenerative therapy by looking back on our research extending over 50 years since 1971. DHEAS is the most abundant circulating steroid hormone in humans and apes. DHEAS is essential for brain development in adrenarche and for anti-aging in adrenopause as shown by the evolutionary process in primates. The molecular mechanisms of action of DHEA and DHEAS have been clarified by the discovery of many membrane receptors and by the concept of intracrinological action, which is especially important in menopausal women. The genes associated with serum DHEAS concentrations were identified by genome-wide association study meta-analysis of cohort studies. Recent advances in aging research have shown that DHEA and DHEAS have anti-aging action via antioxidants, anti-inflammation, telomere protection, p38MAPK inhibition, anti-cortisol effects, and chaperone induction. DHEA has beneficial effects on the prevention of atherosclerosis based on visceral obesity-induced metabolic syndrome in middle-aged people. DHEA also prevents infection, frailty via reverse metabolism, sarcopenia, and osteoporosis in older people, with a marked decrease in serum DHEAS concentrations. This review discusses adrenal regenerative therapy using steroid-producing cell replacement by overexpressing Ad4BP/steroidogenic factor 1 in mouse or human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. This therapy replaces cortisol and DHEAS treatment for the prevention of sudden death by adrenal crisis and severe infection in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease).

Keywords: Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, Adrenarche, Adrenopause, Anti-aging, Adrenal regenerative therapy
sections.introduction:
Butenandt, who was a Nobel Prize winner for the isolation and crystallization of estrone (E 1 ), first discovered DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) in human urine in 1934 [ 1 ]. DHEAS (dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate) was then discovered in human blood by Munson et al. [ 2 ], followed by the discovery of DHEA and DHEAS in human blood by Migeon et al. [ 3 ]. The development of a radioimmunoassay to measure serum DHEAS concentrations by Sekihara et al. [ 4 ] led to the rapid progress of DHEAS research. DHEAS, which is an adrenal androgen, is the most abundant circulating C19 steroid hormone, and >90% of DHEAS is synthesized in the adrenal gland. The half-life of DHEA is approximately 15–30 minutes in blood. However, the half-life of DHEAS is approximately 18–26 hours, resulting in serum DHEAS concentrations of 700-fold higher than those of DHEA.

Serum DHEAS concentrations show a characteristic change over the course of human life ( Fig. 1 ). High serum DHEAS concentrations are observed at birth via high secretion of DHEAS by the fetal adrenal gland. A marked fall in serum DHEAS concentrations to undetectable levels is observed at postpartum. DHEAS concentrations increase at 6–10 years of age in adrenarche, peak at 20 years of age, and then linearly decline at 80–90 years of age, dropping to only 10%–20% of those in young adults in adrenopause [ 5 - 8 ]. DHEAS is important in human life history as shown by the evolutionary process of primates [ 9 ]. The mechanism of the increase in serum DHEAS concentrations in adrenarche and the decrease in serum DHEAS concentrations in adrenopause depend on an increase in cortisol and cytochrome b5 concentrations in adrenocortical cells along with an increase in serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) and leptin concentrations in adrenarche, and a decrease in progenitor stem cells, telomere shorting, and a decrease in antioxidants and cytochrome b5 in adrenocortical cells in adrenopause.

The genes at or near the single nucleotide polymorphisms associated with serum DHEAS concentrations were identified by a genome-wide association study meta-analysis of cohort studies [ 10 , 11 ]. These genes include ZKSCAN5 [ 10 ] and ZNF789 [ 11 ] on chromosome 7, which encode zinc finger proteins and Kruppel family members, and are crucial in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival [ 12 ]. Furthermore, these genes include transcription factors of the cytochrome p450 (CYP) 3A7 promoter, which is involved in polymorphism of the CYP3A7 promoter, and this is associated with low serum DHEAS concentrations [ 13 ]. Other genes associated with serum DHEAS concentrations are as follows: BCL2L11 on chromosome 2 and BMF on chromosome 15, which are involved in anti-apoptosis; ARPCIA on chromosome 7, which is involved in actin filament assembly; CYP2C9 on chromosome 10 and TRIM4 on chromosome 7, which are involved in drug and toxin metabolism in the liver; SULT2A on chromosome 19, which is involved in DHEA sulfation; and HHEX on chromosome 10, which is involved in type 2 diabetes. These findings suggest that aging underlies the genetic regulation of serum DHEAS concentrations.

Recent advances in aging research [ 14 ] have shown that DHEA and DHEAS exhibit anti-aging and longevity effects via antioxidants, anti-inflammation [ 15 ], protection of telomeres, and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38MAPK) inhibition to suppress senescence-associated secretary phenotype (SASP) formation, anti-cortisol effects [ 16 ], and chaperone (heat shock protein [HSP]70, HSP47, and sigma-1 receptor) induction [ 17 ]. Progress for the mechanism of DHEA action has also been made in the discovery of many membrane DHEA receptors, which include G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) on vascular endothelial cells, G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER) on hepatocytes, tyrosine kinase A membrane receptor (TrkAR) on neurons, and γ-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA A ), N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA), Sigma-1, and microtuble-associated protein 2 (Map2) receptors in the brain [ 18 ].

Labrie proposed the concept of intracrinology in which DHEA that is converted from DHEAS by sulfatase in the plasma membrane is transformed into E 1 , estradiol (E 2 ), Δ5Adiol and 3β-Adiol as ligands that bind to estrogen receptors (ER), and testosterone (T) and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) as ligands that bind to androgen receptors (AR) in the cells of peripheral target tissues of the liver, muscle, bone, skin, brain, mammary gland, and prostate by the tissue-specific gene expression of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD), 17β-HSDs, 5α-reductase, and aromatase ( Fig. 2 ) [ 19 , 20 ]. This concept is important in older people, especially menopausal women. In women, E 2 secretion by the ovary stops at menopause. After menopause, 100% of estrogen and androgen are derived from adrenal DHEAS. In older men with decreased T secretion by the testis, 50% of androgen is derived from adrenal DHEAS. Baulieu proposed the concept of a neurosteroid in which DHEAS is synthesized in the central nervous system in the brain and improves memory and learning ability in aged rats [ 21 ].

In in vitro and in vivo studies on rodents and humans, we identified the beneficial effects of DHEA against obesity, diabetes, atherosclerosis, osteoporosis, and dementia, as well as stimulating the immune system [ 7 ]. In humans, Morales and Yen first reported that DHEA supplementation in older people induced an improvement in the sense of well-being and an increase in serum IGF-1 concentrations [ 22 ]. Other studies showed that DHEA supplementation in middle-aged and older people decreased visceral obesity, increased insulin sensitivity [ 23 ], improved glucose tolerance, and reduced serum high-sensitivity C-reactive protein concentrations [ 24 , 25 ]. Prospective cohort studies in middle-aged people showed that DHEA had beneficial effects on the prevention of atherosclerosis by visceral obesity-induced metabolic syndrome [ 26 ]. In older people with a marked decrease in serum DHEAS concentrations, which attenuated the intracrinological action of DHEAS, DHEA supplementation showed beneficial effects on infection, frailty under malnutrition and chronic inflammation due to reverse metabolism, sarcopenia, and osteoporosis in geriatric syndrome [ 26 ].

Cohort studies of patients with Addison’s disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) have shown high mortality due to adrenal crisis and infection [ 27 ]. We succeeded in making adrenal steroid hormone-producing cells by expressing Ad4BP/steroidogenic factor 1 (SF-1) in mouse or human mesenchymal stem cells for supplementation of cortisol and DHEA concentrations to prevent sudden death by adrenal crisis and infection in patients with Addison’s disease.

In this review, we summarize the recent progress of the molecular mechanisms of adrenarche, adrenopause, anti-aging by DHEA and DHEAS, and the beneficial effects of DHEA in older people. We also summarize recent studies on the regeneration of adrenal steroid hormone-producing cells for clinical application in treating Addison’s disease.
sections.conclusion: We reviewed the importance of adrenarche and adrenopause in the human life history as shown by the evolutionary process of primates to explain human longevity. We also discussed the recent progress of molecular mechanisms of anti-aging and beneficial effects of the adrenal androgens DHEA and DHEAS on the prevention of atherosclerosis based on visceral obesity-induced metabolic syndrome and on older people. Finally, we discussed adrenal regenerative therapy in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease). (Please see Graphical Abstract ).
